patient.chief_complaint: Pregnant patient (28 weeks) brought by husband - continuous generalized seizure 10 minutes, not stopping
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Kim is a 35-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation with generalized epilepsy well-controlled on lamotrigine who is brought by her husband after developing a continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure that has lasted 10 minutes. She was eating dinner when she suddenly lost consciousness and began convulsing. She had not had a seizure for 2 years before this pregnancy. Her neurologist increased lamotrigine to 300 mg twice daily during pregnancy after noting declining levels. She had a lamotrigine level drawn 2 weeks ago which was 4.2 mcg/mL (low end of therapeutic). She is at 28 weeks gestation — this is a high-risk obstetric situation. The differential includes: (1) breakthrough SE from subtherapeutic lamotrigine (pregnancy increases lamotrigine clearance by up to 50-300%), (2) eclampsia (must be considered in all pregnant women with new seizures even though this patient has a known seizure disorder), (3) other structural or metabolic causes. Her blood pressure on the floor was reportedly 162/102 per her husband who used their home monitor. Eclampsia cannot be excluded without blood pressure measurement and urine protein assessment. She is 28 weeks — fetal viability is established and fetal monitoring is mandatory. Obstetrics must be involved immediately.

output.query: Eclampsia HELLP syndrome management delivery magnesium timing

results.finding: Eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV loading + 2 g/h maintenance for seizure prophylaxis
HELLP syndrome with platelets <100 + seizures: delivery is definitive treatment
At 28 weeks with HELLP: deliver if platelets <50 or organ failure; stabilize if >50 and viable fetus
BP control: labetalol IV or hydralazine IV for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy
Avoid nimodipine in pregnancy - teratogenic; magnesium sulfate is preferred for eclampsia

output.summary: Eclampsia management: magnesium sulfate 4–6 g IV loading then 2 g/h maintenance for seizure prophylaxis. HELLP syndrome with platelets below 50 or progressive organ failure at viable gestational age is generally an indication for delivery. Acute severe hypertension in pregnancy is managed with IV labetalol or IV hydralazine. Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity is indicated when preterm delivery is anticipated. Nimodipine is not recommended in pregnancy. Multidisciplinary management is standard for eclampsia with HELLP.
